subject: chemistry

items.q: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, undergoes complete combustion in oxygen. What amount of oxygen, O₂, reacts with 1.00 mol of ethanol?
items.correct: 3.00 mol
items.misconception: 3.50 mol
items.why:
Combustion equations are first practised with hydrocarbons, where every O atom in the products does come from O₂. The routine 'count the O atoms in the products and halve' is carried over to alcohols without adjusting it. Count O atoms on both sides. For ethanol the products 2CO₂ + 3H₂O contain 7 O atoms; ethanol provides 1, so O₂ must provide 6, which is 3 O₂.

Working: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). O atoms in products = 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 7; O atoms in 1 C₂H₅OH = 1; O atoms from O₂ = 7 − 1 = 6; amount of O₂ = 6/2 = 3 per mol ethanol, so n(O₂) = 3.00 mol.
items.specStatementText: Reactive metals, non-metals and organic compounds undergo combustion reactions when heated in oxygen.
items.working: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l). O atoms in products = 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 7; O atoms in 1 C₂H₅OH = 1; O atoms from O₂ = 7 − 1 = 6; amount of O₂ = 6/2 = 3 per mol ethanol, so n(O₂) = 3.00 mol.

items.q: Which equation correctly represents the combustion of an element in excess oxygen?
items.correct: P₄(s) + 5O₂(g) → P₄O₁₀(s)
items.misconception: 2Al(s) + O₂(g) → 2AlO(s)
items.why: The first metal oxides students meet, MgO and CaO, are 1 : 1, and the pattern is generalized instead of deducing each formula from the charges of the ions. Deduce the formula of an ionic oxide from the ion charges so that the total charge is zero: Na⁺ gives Na₂O, Mg²⁺ gives MgO, Al³⁺ gives Al₂O₃.
items.specStatementText: Reactive metals, non-metals and organic compounds undergo combustion reactions when heated in oxygen.

items.q: Which equation represents an incomplete combustion of ethanol?
items.correct: C₂H₅OH(l) + O₂(g) → 2C(s) + 3H₂O(l)
items.misconception: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)
items.why: In everyday language 'incomplete' means 'not finished', so students picture fuel left over rather than a change in what the carbon forms. Incomplete combustion is defined by its products. Its equations contain CO or C: for example C₂H₅OH(l) + 2O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 3H₂O(l) and CH₄(g) + O₂(g) → C(s) + 2H₂O(l).
items.specStatementText: Incomplete combustion of organic compounds, especially hydrocarbons, leads to the production of carbon monoxide and carbon.

items.q: Methane burns in a limited supply of oxygen. Which equation represents an incomplete combustion of methane?
items.correct: CH₄(g) + O₂(g) → C(s) + 2H₂O(l)
items.misconception: CH₄(g) + 3O(g) → CO(g) + 2H₂O(l)
items.why: For most elements (metals, carbon, sulfur) the formula is simply the symbol, so students write O and H the same way. When counting atoms during balancing they then equate O atoms with O₂ molecules. Write the diatomic elements as H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. After counting the O atoms needed, divide by two to get the number of O₂ molecules.
items.specStatementText: Incomplete combustion of organic compounds, especially hydrocarbons, leads to the production of carbon monoxide and carbon.

items.q: Coal has a greater tendency than natural gas to undergo incomplete combustion. Which statement gives a reason for this?
items.correct: Coal is a solid, so oxygen reaches only its surface, whereas gas mixes fully with air.
items.misconception: Coal contains impurities, and these, not its carbon, form the soot and carbon monoxide.
items.why: Black smoke is associated with 'dirty' fuels and pollution, so it is read as contamination. Students do not connect the black solid with the carbon in the fuel's formula. Even pure methane or ethanol forms CO and soot when the oxygen supply is limited, as their incomplete-combustion equations show. Impurities such as sulfur produce other pollutants (SO₂), not the soot.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
items.random_wrong: Coal needs more oxygen per gram than methane, as only the carbon in a fuel uses up oxygen.

items.q: Octane, C₈H₁₈, is a component of petrol, which is refined from crude oil. Use the following data: 5470 kJ of energy is released when 1 mol of octane burns completely; A_r: H 1.01, C 12.01, O 16.00. What mass of CO₂ is added to the atmosphere for every 1.00 × 10³ kJ of energy released by burning octane?
items.why:
The word equation 'fuel + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water' is learned without coefficients, so the fuel : CO₂ ratio is taken as 1 : 1. Ignoring the mole ratio is a common error in chemistry calculations. Use the balanced equation: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O, so octane : CO₂ = 1 : 8.

Working: M(CO₂) = 12.01 + 2 × 16.00 = 44.01 g mol⁻¹. 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O, so n(CO₂) : n(C₈H₁₈) = 8 : 1. Per 1 mol octane: m(CO₂) = 8 × 44.01 = 352.08 g for 5470 kJ. Per 1.00 × 10³ kJ: 352.08 × (1000/5470) = 64.37 g ≈ 64.4 g.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.

items.q: Use the following data for the energy released when 1 mol of each fuel burns completely: coal (modelled as pure carbon, C) 394 kJ; natural gas (methane, CH₄) 891 kJ; petrol (modelled as octane, C₈H₁₈) 5470 kJ. A_r: H 1.01, C 12.01, O 16.00. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: Methane releases the most energy per gram of the three fuels.
items.misconception: Octane releases the most energy per gram of the three fuels.
items.why:
Energy data are usually tabulated per mole, and a bigger number is read as a 'better fuel' without dividing by molar mass. Larger molecules release more energy per mole simply because each molecule contains more atoms. To compare fuels per unit mass, divide the energy released per mole by the molar mass of each fuel before comparing.

Working: M: C 12.01; CH₄ 12.01 + 4 × 1.01 = 16.05; C₈H₁₈ 8 × 12.01 + 18 × 1.01 = 114.26 g mol⁻¹. Energy per gram: C 394/12.01 = 32.8; CH₄ 891/16.05 = 55.5; C₈H₁₈ 5470/114.26 = 47.9 kJ g⁻¹. CO₂ per kJ (M(CO₂) = 44.01 g mol⁻¹): C 1 × 44.01/394 = 0.112; CH₄ 1 × 44.01/891 = 0.0494; C₈H₁₈ 8 × 44.01/5470 = 0.0644 g kJ⁻¹. Methane releases the most energy per gram and the least CO₂ per kJ.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
items.random_wrong: Octane adds the least CO₂ per kJ of energy released of the three.
items.working: M: C 12.01; CH₄ 12.01 + 4 × 1.01 = 16.05; C₈H₁₈ 8 × 12.01 + 18 × 1.01 = 114.26 g mol⁻¹. Energy per gram: C 394/12.01 = 32.8; CH₄ 891/16.05 = 55.5; C₈H₁₈ 5470/114.26 = 47.9 kJ g⁻¹. CO₂ per kJ (M(CO₂) = 44.01 g mol⁻¹): C 1 × 44.01/394 = 0.112; CH₄ 1 × 44.01/891 = 0.0494; C₈H₁₈ 8 × 44.01/5470 = 0.0644 g kJ⁻¹. Methane releases the most energy per gram and the least CO₂ per kJ.

items.q: Burning fossil fuels increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. How does this increase lead to warming of the Earth's surface?
items.correct: CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation emitted by the surface and re-emits some of it back.
items.misconception: CO₂ absorbs visible and ultraviolet light coming from the Sun, heating the air.
items.why: Students know that the Sun heats the Earth and that CO₂ 'traps heat', and they do not distinguish the short-wavelength radiation arriving from the Sun from the longer-wavelength infrared radiation emitted by the surface. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface; the surface emits infrared radiation; CO₂ molecules absorb this infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back to the surface.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
items.random_wrong: CO₂ destroys the ozone layer, so more of the Sun's radiation reaches the surface.

items.q: Biofuels are renewable energy sources, whereas fossil fuels are non-renewable. Which statement gives the defining feature of a renewable energy source?
items.correct: It is replenished naturally at least as fast as it is used.
items.misconception: It can be collected and used again after it has released its energy.
items.why: 'Renewable' is confused with 'reusable' and 'recyclable', words met together in everyday environmental messages. Renewable refers to the rate of replacement: new crops can be grown for biofuel each season, whereas coal, oil and gas took millions of years to form.
items.specStatementText: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
items.random_wrong: It adds no carbon dioxide to the atmosphere overall when used.

items.q: Bioethanol is made by fermenting sugar from sugar cane and is burned as a fuel for vehicles. Which statement about bioethanol as a fuel is correct?
items.correct: All of its carbon was fixed from atmospheric CO₂ by photosynthesis in the cane.
items.misconception: It burns to form water only, so using it as a fuel adds no CO₂ to the atmosphere.
items.why: The label 'green fuel' and the claim that biofuels are 'carbon neutral' are heard as 'they emit no CO₂', a claim about the net cycle being mistaken for a claim about the combustion products. A biofuel's combustion products depend on its formula, not its origin: bioethanol is chemically identical to ethanol made from crude oil and releases the same CO₂ per mole. The possible benefit of a biofuel lies in where its carbon came from.
items.specStatementText: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
items.random_wrong: The CO₂ it releases is exactly balanced by photosynthesis, so its net emission is zero.

items.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, hydrogen gas is supplied to the anode. Which half-equation represents the reaction at the anode?
items.correct: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻
items.misconception: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
items.why: The terms anode/cathode and oxidation/reduction are learned as two separate pairs, and sign conventions differ between electrolytic cells (anode positive) and voltaic cells (anode negative), so students reverse them. Confusion over electrode processes is widely reported in electrochemistry-education research. Link the terms by their initial letters: Anode–Oxidation (both vowels), Cathode–Reduction (both consonants). In a fuel cell the fuel is always oxidized at the anode, losing electrons that flow into the external circuit.
items.specStatementText: A fuel cell can be used to convert chemical energy from a fuel directly to electrical energy.

items.q: In a methanol fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, an aqueous solution of methanol is supplied to the anode. Which equation represents the reaction that occurs at the anode?
items.correct: CH₃OH(aq) + H₂O(l) → CO₂(g) + 6H⁺(aq) + 6e⁻
items.misconception: 2CH₃OH(aq) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 8H⁺(aq) + 8e⁻
items.why: Oxidation is first defined as 'gain of oxygen'. When the electron-transfer definition is introduced later, the older definition persists and is applied to electrode reactions. In electrochemistry, oxidation is loss of electrons. The fuel and oxygen react at separate electrodes, which is what forces the electrons through the external circuit.
items.specStatementText: A fuel cell can be used to convert chemical energy from a fuel directly to electrical energy.

items.q: Plants such as sugar cane, grown to make bioethanol, carry out photosynthesis. Which statement gives the reactants and products of photosynthesis?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and water react to form glucose and oxygen gas.
items.misconception: Glucose reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.
items.why: The two processes involve the same four substances, one being the overall reverse of the other, and they are usually learned side by side; everyday talk of plants 'breathing' blurs them further. Confusion between photosynthesis and respiration is widely reported in biology-education research. Photosynthesis builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy and releases oxygen; respiration breaks glucose down with oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide and water. A plant carries out both.
items.specStatementText: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
items.random_wrong: Water and soil minerals react to form glucose and oxygen.

items.q: When the equation for the complete combustion of octane, C₈H₁₈, is balanced with a coefficient of 2 for octane, what is the coefficient of O₂?
items.why:
Chemistry-education research on students' ideas about burning widely reports that water is not recognized as a combustion product: it leaves as invisible vapour, whereas carbon dioxide dominates public discussion of fuels. Both elements are oxidized: C → CO₂ (or CO, C when oxygen is limited) and H → H₂O. When balancing, the oxygen needed for the water must be counted, and a fuel with a high proportion of hydrogen, such as methane, needs more oxygen per gram than carbon does.

Working: Complete combustion: all carbon → CO₂, all hydrogen → H₂O. 2C₈H₁₈ contains 16 C and 36 H atoms, so the products are 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. O atoms in the products = 16 × 2 + 18 × 1 = 50, supplied by 50/2 = 25 O₂: 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l). (For one octane molecule the coefficient would be 12½, which is why the equation is written for two.)
items.specStatementText: Reactive metals, non-metals and organic compounds undergo combustion reactions when heated in oxygen.
items.working: Complete combustion: all carbon → CO₂, all hydrogen → H₂O. 2C₈H₁₈ contains 16 C and 36 H atoms, so the products are 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. O atoms in the products = 16 × 2 + 18 × 1 = 50, supplied by 50/2 = 25 O₂: 2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l). (For one octane molecule the coefficient would be 12½, which is why the equation is written for two.)

items.q: Use the following data for the energy released when 1 mol of each fuel burns completely: coal (modelled as pure carbon, C) 394 kJ; petrol (modelled as octane, C₈H₁₈) 5470 kJ. A_r: H 1.01, C 12.01, O 16.00. How many times greater is the mass of CO₂ added to the atmosphere per kJ of energy released when coal burns than when octane burns?
items.why:
Everyday language says a fire 'needs air' and fuel 'burns away', which casts oxygen as a helper and hides its mass because it and the gaseous products are invisible. This view of oxygen as an activator rather than a reactant is widely reported in research on students' ideas about combustion. Oxygen is consumed and its atoms are combined in the products. When magnesium burns the solid gains mass; when octane burns, the CO₂ formed has a greater mass than the octane because each CO₂ contains two oxygen atoms from O₂.

Working: M(CO₂) = 12.01 + 2 × 16.00 = 44.01 g mol⁻¹. Coal: C + O₂ → CO₂, 1 mol CO₂ per 394 kJ: 44.01/394 = 0.1117 g kJ⁻¹. Octane: 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O, 8 mol CO₂ per 5470 kJ: 8 × 44.01/5470 = 352.08/5470 = 0.06437 g kJ⁻¹. Ratio = 0.1117/0.06437 = 1.74 (no unit).
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.

items.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which equation represents the reaction that occurs at the cathode?
items.correct: O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l)
items.misconception: H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) + heat
items.why: Fuels are met as substances that are burned, and electricity from fuels is met in power stations that burn fuel to raise steam. The overall equation of a hydrogen fuel cell is the same as the combustion equation of hydrogen, which reinforces the idea. In a fuel cell the two half-reactions happen at different electrodes, so electrons pass through the external circuit instead of being transferred directly in a flame; there is no combustion step.
items.specStatementText: A fuel cell can be used to convert chemical energy from a fuel directly to electrical energy.

items.q: Can a combustion equation be balanced by changing a formula, for example writing H₂O₂ for the product of burning hydrogen?
items.correct: No. The formula identifies the substance; changing a subscript describes a different substance. Balance by changing coefficients only: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l).
items.misconception: An equation can be balanced by changing the subscripts in a formula until the atoms add up.
items.why: Changing a subscript makes the atom count match at once and seems the quickest fix. Students who see balancing as an arithmetic puzzle do not yet connect the formula with the identity of a substance. Keep every formula fixed and change only the numbers in front of formulae. Hydrogen burns to water, H₂O; hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, is a different substance and is not the combustion product.
items.specStatementText: Reactive metals, non-metals and organic compounds undergo combustion reactions when heated in oxygen.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does burning natural gas add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
items.correct: Yes. Methane contains carbon, so it forms CO₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O), and it forms CO and soot if the oxygen supply is limited. It releases less CO₂ per unit energy than coal or oil, but not zero.
items.misconception: Natural gas is a clean fuel: it burns to water and produces no carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide or soot.
items.why: Natural gas is marketed as 'clean-burning', and its blue flame leaves no visible smoke or ash, so 'cleaner' is heard as 'no carbon emissions'. Every carbon-containing fuel releases CO₂ on complete combustion. Natural gas is cleaner than coal in releasing less CO₂ per kJ and less soot, but it is still a fossil fuel that adds CO₂ to the atmosphere.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the mass of CO₂ produced by a fuel the same as the mass of carbon in it?
items.correct: No. Each carbon atom (12.01 g mol⁻¹) becomes a CO₂ molecule (44.01 g mol⁻¹), so the mass of CO₂ is 44.01/12.01 ≈ 3.7 times the mass of carbon burned.
items.misconception: The mass of CO₂ produced is equal to the mass of carbon in the fuel, since 'carbon emissions' and 'CO₂ emissions' mean the same thing.
items.why: Emissions are reported both as 'tonnes of carbon' and 'tonnes of CO₂', and talk of a 'carbon footprint' blurs the two, so students use the mass of carbon atoms where the mass of CO₂ molecules is needed. Convert the amount of carbon to the amount of CO₂ (1 : 1) and multiply by M(CO₂) = 44.01 g mol⁻¹, not by A_r(C) = 12.01.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the greenhouse effect caused by damage to the ozone layer?
items.correct: No. They are different problems. The greenhouse effect involves absorption of infrared radiation by gases such as CO₂; ozone depletion, caused mainly by CFCs, allows more ultraviolet radiation to reach the surface. CO₂ does not destroy ozone.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide causes global warming by destroying the ozone layer, which lets more of the Sun's heat reach the surface.
items.why: Environmental problems are met together in the media and in school, often as 'pollution damaging the atmosphere', and chemistry-education research widely reports that students merge the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion. Keep the two mechanisms separate: CO₂ warms the surface by absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation; ozone depletion is a separate effect on ultraviolet radiation.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does carbon dioxide warm the Earth by reflecting heat back to the surface?
items.correct: No. CO₂ molecules absorb infrared radiation emitted by the surface and re-emit it in all directions; they do not form a reflecting layer.
items.misconception: Greenhouse gases form a layer high in the atmosphere that reflects heat back down to the Earth, like a mirror or the glass of a greenhouse.
items.why: The 'blanket' and 'greenhouse glass' analogies, and diagrams showing arrows bouncing off a band in the sky, suggest a reflecting layer. Research on students' ideas about the greenhouse effect widely reports this picture. Greenhouse gases are mixed throughout the atmosphere. Their molecules absorb infrared radiation, gaining energy, and re-emit infrared in all directions, so some returns to the surface.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a renewable fuel add no carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
items.correct: No. A renewable fuel such as bioethanol releases CO₂ when it burns, and fossil fuels used to grow, transport and process it add more. Whether a source is renewable depends on how fast it is replenished, not on its emissions.
items.misconception: Renewable fuels are carbon neutral: the CO₂ released when they burn is exactly balanced by the CO₂ the plants absorbed, so their net effect on atmospheric CO₂ is zero.
items.why: Biofuels are promoted as 'green' and 'carbon neutral', and the simple cycle 'plants absorb CO₂, burning returns it' leaves out the energy used in farming and processing. The carbon cycle of the crop itself is roughly balanced, but fuel for machinery, fertilizer manufacture, transport and fermentation or refining adds CO₂, and land clearing can release more. Biofuels can reduce net CO₂ emissions, but not to zero.
items.specStatementText: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any energy source that comes from nature renewable?
items.correct: No. Coal, crude oil and natural gas are natural and formed from the remains of plants and other organisms, yet they are non-renewable because they formed over millions of years and are used far faster than they form.
items.misconception: An energy source is renewable if it is natural or comes from living things, such as plants or animals.
items.why: 'Natural' and 'renewable' are both used as positive labels in everyday language, and biofuels are introduced as fuels 'from plants', so the biological origin is taken as the defining feature. Classify by the rate of replenishment, not by origin: biofuels are renewable because new biomass grows within months or years; fossil fuels are non-renewable although they are also biological in origin.
items.specStatementText: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the carbon in plant material, and so in a biofuel, come from?
items.correct: From carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, fixed by photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. The roots take up water and mineral ions, not the carbon.
items.misconception: Plants take their carbon, and most of their mass, from the soil through their roots.
items.why: Plants visibly grow out of soil and are 'fed' with fertilizer, and a gas seems too insubstantial to build a solid plant. This idea is one of the most widely reported misconceptions in research on students' understanding of photosynthesis. Almost all the carbon in biomass comes from atmospheric CO₂, taken in through the leaves and converted to glucose by photosynthesis. That is why the carbon released when a biofuel burns was only recently removed from the air.
items.specStatementText: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does hydrogen gain electrons at the anode of a hydrogen fuel cell, like other non-metals?
items.correct: No. At the anode hydrogen loses electrons and forms H⁺ ions: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. Hydrogen is oxidized.
items.misconception: Hydrogen is a non-metal, and non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions, so hydrogen forms H⁻ ions in the cell.
items.why: The rule 'metals lose electrons, non-metals gain electrons' is learned from ionic bonding and applied to hydrogen, which has oxidation state +1 in most of its compounds and forms H⁺(aq) in acids (it forms H⁻ ions only in the hydrides of very reactive metals). In a fuel cell hydrogen is the fuel and is oxidized: it loses electrons at the anode, forming H⁺(aq), which moves through the acidic electrolyte to the cathode.
items.specStatementText: A fuel cell can be used to convert chemical energy from a fuel directly to electrical energy.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In photosynthesis, is carbon dioxide split into carbon, which the plant keeps, and oxygen, which it releases?
items.correct: No. Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form glucose and oxygen. The carbon of CO₂ becomes part of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, whose hydrogen comes from water; no elemental carbon is formed.
items.misconception: In photosynthesis the plant splits carbon dioxide, keeping the carbon and releasing the oxygen, so the products are carbon and oxygen and water plays no part in the reaction.
items.why: Photosynthesis is often summarized as 'plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen', which suggests that the oxygen of CO₂ is simply let go and the carbon left behind; water uptake is taught separately, under transport. Treating photosynthesis as a conversion of carbon dioxide into oxygen is widely reported in research on students' ideas about photosynthesis. Count the atoms: glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, contains hydrogen as well as carbon and oxygen, and the hydrogen can only come from water, which is therefore a reactant. The products are glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
items.specStatementText: Biofuels are produced from the biological fixation of carbon over a short period of time through photosynthesis.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the mass of CO₂ formed per gram of fuel a fair way to compare how much CO₂ different fuels add for the energy they supply?
items.correct: No. Fuels release different amounts of energy per gram, so they must be compared per unit of energy released (e.g. g of CO₂ per kJ): divide the mass of CO₂ formed per mole of fuel by the energy released per mole.
items.misconception: The mass of CO₂ formed per gram of fuel burned is a fair measure of the CO₂ added per unit of energy, as if every fuel released the same energy per gram.
items.why: CO₂ emissions are commonly quoted per tonne or per litre of fuel, so the mass of fuel becomes the default basis for comparison, and the energy each gram supplies is left out. It is the same basis error as comparing fuels by energy per mole instead of per gram. Fix the basis first. To compare CO₂ added for the same energy demand, work out the mass of CO₂ per kJ for each fuel: (moles of CO₂ per mole of fuel × 44.01 g mol⁻¹) ÷ energy released per mole of fuel.
items.specStatementText: Fossil fuels include coal, crude oil and natural gas, which have different advantages and disadvantages.
